abstract: |
  **Purpose:** Morning and evening chronotypes may encounter light at different clock times. Prior studies also suggest phase-specific exposure patterns that could counter further advances in early types and delays in late types. We examined whether photoperiod modifies these exposure patterns in a direction compatible with counteracting timing extremes.

  **Methods:** We analysed near-eye melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) in 140 participants from the MeLiDos cohort across seven countries (778 participant-days; 35,949 half-hour observations). Cyclic generalized additive mixed models compared four quartiles of midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc) in clock time and relative to MSFsc, accounting for day type, site, photoperiod and individual patterns. Exploratory analyses tested daylength moderation and used phase-response-curve (PRC) weighting as a conceptual comparison of exposure timing.

  **Results:** Modelled extreme evening-type/morning-type exposure ratios averaged 0.16 (95% CI 0.06–0.40) 9.6–11.3 hours before MSFsc (pre-MSFsc) and 14.0 (5.6–34.8) 0.9–4.4 hours after MSFsc (post-MSFsc). The models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R² (0.795 for clock time; 0.794 for MSFsc-relative time). Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days, with the pre-MSFsc contrast descriptively attenuated on free days. The post-MSFsc ratio increased by a factor of 2.59 (95% CI 1.06–6.34) between civil photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with no significant moderation of the pre-MSFsc contrast. A sensitivity using a diary-derived correlate of MSFsc did not show significant post-MSFsc moderation. Conceptual PRC weighting gave higher advance-weighted exposure indices in extreme evening than extreme morning types, with an uncertain group difference (drift-corrected index difference 0.15; 95% CI −0.11 to 0.40).

  **Conclusions:** Extreme chronotypes differed in daily exposure both in clock time and relative to MSFsc. The established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure showed significant post-MSFsc daylength moderation; its diary-derived correlate did not. The opposite pre-MSFsc contrast showed no clear moderation. The exposure patterns and conceptual PRC comparison suggest a possible pathway linking daylight availability to entrainment in extreme chronotypes.

## Introduction

Daily timing and light exposure are closely connected: sleep and activity schedules influence when people encounter light, while light contributes to entrainment. Chronotype-related differences in exposure relative to circadian phase are particularly relevant because light can advance or delay the clock depending on when it occurs.[@sthilaire2012] Everyday exposure also depends on the solar day, indoor environments and social schedules.[@zauner2026exposome] Comparing groups at the same clock time shows when their light environments differ. Comparing them at the same circadian phase asks whether they receive different light input at equivalent points in their biological day.

Goulet and colleagues compared morning and evening types in clock time and in circadian phase anchored to measured dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO).[@goulet2007] Participants were classified using the Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ).[@horne1976] In the full analytical sample of 19 participants, the clock-time differences were no longer statistically detectable after DLMO alignment. In a subset with extreme DLMO timing, comprising four morning and five evening types, morning types received more light around DLMO, whereas evening types received more light 10–12 hours later. The authors suggested that this exposure pattern could help stabilize entrainment: light near DLMO could delay early types and counter further advances, whereas light 10–12 hours later could advance late types and counter further delays. This interpretation was consistent with proposed differences in intrinsic circadian period, which the study did not measure. Its small subgroup and selected sleep schedules leave open how consistently the pattern occurs in everyday life.

Emens and colleagues combined seven days of wrist light measurements with plasma DLMO in 66 MEQ-defined morning and evening types.[@emens2009] Their subgroups with non-overlapping circadian phases comprised morning types whose DLMO occurred earlier than every evening type and evening types whose DLMO occurred later than every morning type. Evening types in these subgroups had a higher advance-to-delay ratio of log-transformed light exposure than morning types, indicating relatively more light in the phase-advancing than phase-delaying region. Their interpretation extended Goulet's suggestion that phase-specific exposure could help stabilize entrainment.

Daylight availability might contribute to these differences. When melatonin onset occurs earlier in the solar day, daylight may still be available around that phase; people with later melatonin onset may reach the same phase after dusk. Natural-light studies show that changes in the light environment can alter circadian timing and that seasonal daylight changes are relevant to human entrainment.[@wright2013; @stothard2017] Photoperiod could therefore alter the exposure that counteracts early or late timing.

We examined these patterns in a dataset originating from the multicentre MeLiDos study of personal light exposure.[@zauner2026exposome] We compared four chronotype groups using local clock time and time relative to midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc). MSFsc provides a sleep-based proxy for aligning exposure to circadian phase, distinct from the melatonin-based DLMO measure used by Goulet and colleagues.[@roenneberg2015; @kantermann2015; @reiter2021] We first asked whether chronotype differences remain after this alignment and whether they differ between work and free days. Two post hoc analyses then examined how photoperiod modifies the extreme-group contrast and whether weighting by a light phase-response curve (PRC) places extreme evening types in a more phase-advancing direction than extreme morning types. Together, these analyses extend the entrainment interpretation proposed in the Goulet and Emens studies by testing photoperiod as a possible contributor.[@goulet2007; @emens2009]

## Methods

### Study and measurements

This analysis used prepared light and diary data from the MeLiDos study and its archived analysis repository.[@zauner2026exposome; @melidosanalysis2026] Measurements were collected from August 2023 to October 2025 at nine sites in seven countries using a common protocol. Recruitment occurred through the participating research groups. The source study's daily-pattern analysis and preregistration are described elsewhere [@melidos2026preregistration]; the daylength and PRC analyses reported here were exploratory additions after inspection of the primary chronotype results.

Participants followed an eight-day ambulatory protocol with spectrally sensitive ActLumus loggers recording every 10 seconds.[@guidolin2024] The outcome was melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melanopic EDI), which expresses melanopsin-weighted light as the illuminance of an equivalent daylight spectrum, in lux.[@cie2018s026] Near-eye recordings were primary; concurrent chest recordings provided a placement sensitivity analysis. During recorded sleep, devices were placed near the bed, so those observations represent the sleeping environment rather than near-eye exposure. Declared waking non-wear was treated as unavailable. Eligible days required at least 80% valid coverage of the combined waking and bedside-sleep record, excluding wholly zero days. The analysis used prepared 30-minute arithmetic means, requiring at least 15 valid minutes per bin. Remaining zero values were retained, and the response was log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1). This transformation accommodates darkness (0 lux) while retaining variation over the wide range of personal light exposure.[@zauner2025zeros]

The prepared near-eye data comprised 141 participants and 816 participant-days. Missing MSFsc excluded one participant and six days; missing waking-date diary records excluded a further 32 days. The common sample for both time coordinates comprised 140 participants, 778 participant-days and 35,949 half-hour observations. Work/free-day labels came from the diary for the waking date. The [online supplement](analysis.qmd) documents source preprocessing, inclusion, model specifications, diagnostics and all sensitivity analyses.

### Chronotype and time coordinates

Participants were assigned to MSFsc quartiles using one value per person. Boundaries were 03:10, 04:16 and 05:15; ties remained in the earlier quartile. We label the quartiles extreme morning, moderate morning, moderate evening and extreme evening, respectively. These labels describe relative positions within this sample. The Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) provided a sensitivity classification.[@horne1976] Because only three participants were definite evening types, we combined definite and moderate types within each morning-type/evening-type group, excluding intermediate types from this sensitivity only.

Clock time was the local midpoint of each half-hour bin. The second coordinate subtracted the participant's MSFsc and wrapped the result over 24 hours. Negative values therefore precede corrected midsleep. MSFsc was not a daily observation of sleep status: a plotted time after MSFsc does not establish that a participant was asleep or awake then.

DLMO was not measured. For interpretation, we show an external guide spanning 6.95–5.95 hours before MSFsc, derived from the early- and late-group means reported by Facer-Childs and colleagues.[@facerchilds2019] Its midpoint, 6.45 hours before MSFsc, anchors the central PRC calculation. The guide does not estimate individual DLMO; questionnaire-based chronotype and DLMO are related but can differ substantially.[@kantermann2015; @reiter2021]

### Diary midsleep relative to MSFsc

In a separate descriptive analysis, we compared MSFsc with the midpoint between diary-reported sleep onset and final awakening. Each sleep episode inherited the work/free-day label of its waking date. We included all valid diary nights from the primary participants, including nights without usable light observations. Pearson correlations were calculated overall and by day type, with 95% intervals from 2,000 participant-level bootstrap samples that retained each person's nights together. Correlations of participant means provided an equal-participant sensitivity. We also calculated a diary-derived MSFsc equivalent (dMSFsc) by correcting mean free-day midsleep for sleep debt, using the observed work/free-day night counts to weight mean sleep duration. This calculation required at least one night of each type. Within-person midsleep standard deviations required at least three nights in the relevant day-type context. Calculations used local clock time with midnight handled continuously; the supplement gives the correction formula and an elapsed-time sensitivity for daylight-saving transitions.

A separate [dMSFsc sensitivity](diary-msfsc-sensitivity.qmd) repeated the exposure models and downstream analyses using the diary-derived correlate and its quartiles. The established questionnaire measure remained primary. A questionnaire-MSFsc repeat on exactly the same eligible participants and light observations separated changes in timing and classification from sample restriction.

### Daily exposure models and comparisons

We fitted Gaussian generalized additive mixed models separately for clock time and time relative to MSFsc, using identical observations. Cyclic smooths represented the common daily pattern, chronotype quartiles, work/free days and their interaction, site differences and individual daily curves. Participant-day intercepts captured day-to-day variation. Common photoperiod terms allowed exposure to vary with civil daylength, defined from dawn to dusk at a solar elevation of −6° and centered on each site's average photoperiod over observed dates. Models were fitted in R 4.6.1 using `mgcv` and fast restricted maximum likelihood.[@wood2017; @wood2017large] An AR(1) correction followed actual elapsed time and reset at participant-day boundaries, missing intervals and ambiguous daylight-saving links.

For standardized group predictions, site, participant and participant-day effects were set to zero. Predictions averaged over a common photoperiod distribution, with equal weight per participant and equal weight per observed day within participant. Overall curves used the same pooled work/free-day mixture in every group. Exposure curves were back-transformed standardized log-scale means, not arithmetic mean lux. Their 95% simultaneous bands covered all 12 quartile-by-day-context curves and 144 time points within each coordinate, using the same 10,000 joint coefficient draws and smoothing-parameter-adjusted covariance as the contrast bands below. Exposure was plotted on an axis linear up to 1 lux and logarithmic above it.[@zauner2025zeros]

The primary comparisons comprised chronotype direction, chronotype strength, day type and their interactions. We formed 95% simultaneous bands from 10,000 joint coefficient draws over the full registered family of 20 contrasts and all times within each coordinate, separately from the exposure-curve family. Clock-time comparisons describe differences in the daily light environment; MSFsc-relative comparisons ask whether those differences remain after sleep-timing alignment. These separate questions follow the clock-time and phase-aligned comparisons in the literature, so coverage was controlled separately within each coordinate.[@goulet2007] Interval claims additionally required four participants in every contributing quartile/day-type cell locally.

Exponentiated log contrasts compare **melanopic EDI + 0.1**. A ratio of one indicates no difference between the compared groups or conditions; a confidence interval excluding one supports a difference. Ratios averaged over an interval are geometric means of the phase-specific ratios. Interval-average 95% confidence intervals used the full coefficient covariance for the mean log contrast, including smoothing-parameter uncertainty, before exponentiation. They treat selected windows as fixed, without multiplicity or selection adjustment, and are distinct from the simultaneous bands used to identify the windows.

We evaluated prediction using five participant-held-out folds and, separately, a held-out final day for eligible participants. Shapley allocations divided the increase in ordinary in-sample R² above the common daily curve among model components by averaging their additional contributions across subset models.[@azen2003] These allocations were conditional on the fitted models and describe their decomposition rather than independent biological contributions. Sensitivity analyses examined chest placement, alternative smooth boundaries, residual-variance weighting and MEQ classification; details are in the supplement. Chest and noncyclic comparisons used the same within-coordinate coverage rule. MEQ sensitivity bands jointly covered overall, work-day and free-day contrasts within each coordinate and classification.

### Exploratory daylength moderation

We added a quartile-specific change in the daily curve per hour of site-centered photoperiod to the full MSFsc-relative model. This change was linear in photoperiod and common to work and free days. The principal comparison used photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with that average as an intermediate reference. We estimated extreme evening-type/extreme morning-type ratios at these targets and their longer-day/shorter-day ratio of ratios.

Daylength inference used pointwise 95% intervals and interval-average contrasts within the two intervals selected by the primary model. The latter treated those intervals as fixed and were not adjusted for multiplicity or interval selection. Local support required four participants in each extreme-quartile/day-type cell within one hour of the photoperiod target. We also described civil daylight availability relative to MSFsc, with equal participant and within-participant day weights. Its shorter/longer absolute-daylength categories were distinct from the within-site-centered model targets. Matched held-out predictions tested whether moderation improved prediction for new participants.

### Exploratory PRC-weighted exposure

Multiplying daily exposure profiles by a PRC and integrating the result has an ambulatory precedent in Arguelles-Prieto and colleagues.[@arguellesprieto2022] We adapted this approach to compare the timing of modelled melanopic exposure conceptually, without predicting phase shifts.

We weighted the primary model's extreme-group exposure curves by the one-hour bright-white-light PRC of St Hilaire and colleagues.[@sthilaire2012] Numerical coordinates came from the digitized data deposited by Walch and colleagues.[@walch2025amplitude] A two-harmonic curve was reconstructed from 18 responses, using pulse midpoint as the time coordinate. We compared the published raw curve, P, with P + 0.54. In the original protocol, phase shifts were assessed from DLMO measured in constant routines separated by three 24-hour cycles with background light below 3 lux. The assumed mean intrinsic period of 24.18 hours implied a free-running delay of 0.54 hours over this interval; adding 0.54 sets that baseline to zero.[@sthilaire2012]

Each PRC was divided by its integrated absolute area and used to weight log10(melanopic EDI + 0.1) + 1 across 24 hours. Adding one sets zero exposure to zero on the transformed scale. A positive index indicates that exposure is weighted toward the PRC's advance region; a negative index indicates weighting toward its delay region. The index is not calibrated in hours of phase shift. The central alignment placed DLMO 6.45 hours before MSFsc; the guide endpoints at 5.95 and 6.95 hours before MSFsc and two wider offsets provided alignment sensitivities. Coefficient-based 95% intervals retained covariance across time and groups, conditional on the reconstructed PRC and assumed alignment. They did not propagate uncertainty in the external PRC or individual circadian phase.

As a sensitivity analysis, we adapted the advance/delay exposure balance of Emens and colleagues.[@emens2009] We applied log10(melanopic EDI + 1) to back-transformed fitted exposure, setting negative EDI predictions to zero. The mean transformed exposure from 16 to 4 hours before DLMO was divided by the mean from 4 hours before to 8 hours after DLMO. We compared balances in extreme evening and morning types by their ratio at the three guide alignments, using 10,000 joint coefficient draws for unadjusted 95% percentile intervals conditional on the fitted model and assumed DLMO.

## Results

### Sample and chronotype distribution

The four MSFsc groups contained 36, 34, 36 and 34 participants, respectively (@fig-manuscript-chronotypes). The extreme groups contributed 70 participants and 390 participant-days. MEQ scores overlapped across MSFsc quartiles, illustrating that sleep timing and morning/evening preference do not give identical classifications. The MEQ sensitivity analysis retained 68 participants and 379 participant-days after excluding 72 intermediate participants.

![**Chronotype distributions among 140 participants.** (A) MSFsc in 20-minute bins, with quartile boundaries at 03:10, 04:16 and 05:15. (B) MEQ scores in one-point bins, with category boundaries. Colors indicate the same MSFsc quartiles in both panels. Each participant contributes once; participant-day counts describe available exposure records and do not weight the histograms. The 72 intermediate MEQ participants remain in the primary analysis and are excluded only from the MEQ sensitivity.](results/figures/manuscript/figure-1-chronotypes.png){#fig-manuscript-chronotypes fig-alt="Two histograms show corrected free-day midsleep and MEQ scores for the same 140 participants. Four colors identify MSFsc quartiles in both panels. Dashed lines mark quartile boundaries in A and MEQ categories in B; higher MEQ scores indicate greater morning preference."}

### Diary midsleep corresponds with MSFsc but varies across nights

The 140 primary participants contributed 971 valid diary nights: 620 before work days and 351 before free days (@fig-manuscript-diary A). Diary midsleep correlated with MSFsc overall (r = 0.66; 95% CI 0.59–0.73), on work days (r = 0.67; 0.59–0.74) and on free days (r = 0.74; 0.67–0.81). Correlations of participant means were 0.81, 0.75 and 0.82, respectively (@fig-manuscript-diary B). The stronger correlations after averaging nights fit MSFsc's role as a measure of habitual sleep timing rather than an individual night's midpoint. The stronger free-day association is consistent with MSFsc being based on free-day midsleep, with work-day sleep duration contributing to its sleep-debt correction.

Among the 139 participants with at least three nights, the median within-person midsleep SD was 47 minutes (IQR 34–62). Diary midsleep was typically earlier than MSFsc before work days and later before free days, with median differences of −34 and +18 minutes. At the group level, these modest offsets follow the expected work/free-day directions and do not suggest a large, uniform displacement from MSFsc.

For the 135 participants with both work-day and free-day nights, dMSFsc correlated with questionnaire MSFsc at r = 0.79 (95% CI 0.72–0.85; @fig-manuscript-diary C). Its median difference was +6 minutes (IQR −28 to +36), compared with +23 minutes for uncorrected mean free-day midsleep in the same participants. The correction reduced the typical offset, although the correlation was slightly lower than for the uncorrected free-day means (r = 0.82). The [diary side-analysis](analysis.qmd#sec-sleep-diary) gives day-type variability and results using all available participants.

### Alignment to MSFsc broadly reverses the clock-time differences

In clock time, morning-type exposure rose and declined earlier than evening-type exposure (@fig-manuscript-patterns A). Alignment to MSFsc broadly reversed the extreme-group differences in these portions of the daily pattern (@fig-manuscript-patterns B). Extreme morning types had higher fitted exposure approximately 9.6–11.3 hours before MSFsc (pre-MSFsc), with an average extreme evening-type/extreme morning-type ratio of 0.16 (95% CI 0.06–0.40). Extreme evening types had higher exposure approximately 0.9–4.4 hours after MSFsc (post-MSFsc), with an average ratio of 14.0 (95% CI 5.6–34.8). Large ratios during the rising portion of the curve can occur at low absolute exposure.

Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days. The pre-MSFsc evening-type/morning-type ratio was 0.13 on work days and 0.21 on free days, indicating descriptive attenuation on free days. The corresponding post-MSFsc ratios were 15.5 and 12.0. Simultaneous interaction bands did not show a significant difference in the chronotype contrast between day types.

The MEQ sensitivity analysis reproduced the post-MSFsc pattern, with higher evening-type exposure. For the overall comparison, alternative noncyclic group curves retained a significant post-MSFsc difference, whereas the pre-MSFsc band included one. The post-MSFsc contrast was therefore more stable than the pre-MSFsc contrast to the spline specification.

### Fit and prediction

Clock-time and MSFsc-relative models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R², 0.795 and 0.794, respectively. These fit statistics include participant and day effects. Chronotype direction and strength together received Shapley allocations of 0.007 R² in the clock-time model and 0.012 R² in the MSFsc-relative model, above the common daily curve. Individual daily patterns received the largest allocation. Alignment to MSFsc therefore exposed interpretable group differences without making chronotype the dominant source of variation.

Clock time predicted new participants slightly better: predictive R² was 0.668, compared with 0.652 for time relative to MSFsc, and log-scale root mean squared error was 0.887 versus 0.908. The paired root mean squared error difference was 0.0205 (95% CI 0.0108–0.0310). Prediction of a held-out final day for known participants was similar, with predictive R² of 0.674 for clock time and 0.672 for time relative to MSFsc.

### Daylength moderation is clearest post-MSFsc

The extreme-group ratio post-MSFsc increased with photoperiod (@fig-manuscript-daylength A–C). Across the primary post-MSFsc interval, the geometric mean evening-type/morning-type ratio was 7.99 at the −1-hour target and 20.69 at the +1-hour target. Their ratio was 2.59 (95% CI 1.06–6.34). In the pre-MSFsc interval, the ratio of ratios was 0.83 (0.33–2.09), providing no clear evidence of moderation. A separate trough around 8.33 hours before MSFsc had a pointwise estimate of 0.41 (0.16–1.04). A ratio of one indicates no change in the group contrast with photoperiod; this interval included one.

Astronomical daylight occurred at different MSFsc-relative times in the extreme groups (@fig-manuscript-daylength D). Within the pre-MSFsc interval, civil daylight was more available to morning types; within the post-MSFsc interval, it was more available to evening types. These availability gaps were smaller on longer absolute days. These descriptive differences in exposure opportunity do not directly translate to the within-site-centered moderation of measured exposure (@fig-manuscript-daylength A–C).

Adding photoperiod moderation did not improve new-participant prediction. Predictive R² was 0.649 for the expanded model and 0.652 for the primary MSFsc-relative model. The paired root mean squared error difference was 0.0044 (95% CI −0.0008 to 0.0100).

### Evening types trend toward a more phase-advancing exposure pattern than morning types

At the central DLMO alignment, overall indices based on the published raw PRC were −0.152 (95% CI −0.351 to 0.046) for extreme morning types and 0.046 (−0.148 to 0.240) for extreme evening types (@fig-manuscript-prc). Both intervals spanned zero. With the drift-corrected PRC, indices were 1.276 (1.104–1.448) and 1.422 (1.255–1.589), respectively, indicating advance-weighted exposure in both groups.

Extreme groups comprise 70 participants and 390 participant-days. In A, labelled grey bands identify the pre-MSFsc and post-MSFsc intervals, and the striped band shows the external DLMO guide.](results/figures/manuscript/figure-4-prc.png){#fig-manuscript-prc fig-alt="A shows raw and drift-corrected one-hour light PRCs with 18 source points and alignment to corrected midsleep; shaded windows are labelled pre-MSFsc and post-MSFsc. B compares extreme morning and evening weighted exposure indices. Raw-PRC group intervals span zero; drift-corrected group intervals lie above zero. Smooth-PRC direct group contrasts include zero at the central alignment. C shows higher Emens-style advance/delay balances in evening than morning types across day types; its reference line at one denotes equal regional means within a group."}

The extreme evening-type minus morning-type contrast was positive under both baselines: 0.198 (95% CI −0.094 to 0.491) with the raw PRC and 0.146 (−0.106 to 0.398) with drift correction. Every direct group-contrast interval included zero at the central alignment, overall and separately on work and free days. Across the guide alignments at 5.95, 6.45 and 6.95 hours before MSFsc, only the raw-PRC work-day contrast at 6.95 hours before MSFsc narrowly excluded zero, 0.297 (0.002–0.593); all overall contrasts remained uncertain. The relative trend indicates more advance-weighted exposure in evening types than morning types, or more delay-weighted exposure in morning types than evening types, with uncertain group differences.

At the central DLMO alignment, the Emens-style advance/delay balances were 2.43 (95% CI 1.94–3.06) in extreme morning types and 4.28 (3.23–5.71) in extreme evening types (@fig-manuscript-prc C). The evening-type/morning-type ratio of balances was 1.76 (95% CI 1.21–2.58); its overall interval remained above one at both DLMO guide endpoints.

### Diary-derived MSFsc preserves exposure differences but weakens daylength moderation

The matched questionnaire and dMSFsc analyses used 135 participants, 755 participant-days and 34,884 half-hours; 50 participants changed quartile. Within the original phase windows, the extreme evening-type/morning-type ratio was 0.13 (95% CI 0.05–0.33) pre-dMSFsc and 28.3 (11.3–70.9) post-dMSFsc, compared with 0.18 (0.07–0.46) and 14.7 (5.8–37.7) using questionnaire MSFsc on the same observations. These unadjusted interval-average comparisons retained the direction of both exposure differences.

The post-MSFsc longer-day/shorter-day ratio was 2.66 (95% CI 1.10–6.43) in the matched questionnaire analysis, but 1.15 (0.52–2.54) using dMSFsc. Thus daylength moderation was no longer significant with diary-derived timing and groups. The relative PRC-weighted evening-type direction persisted: at the transferred central DLMO alignment, the raw-PRC contrast was 0.306 (0.008–0.604), whereas the drift-corrected contrast was 0.236 (−0.021 to 0.494). The [full sensitivity analysis](diary-msfsc-sensitivity.qmd) reports alignment, prediction, attribution and model-structure comparisons.

## Discussion

We detected significant exposure differences between extreme morning and evening types in both clock time and MSFsc-relative time, but no significant differences between moderate morning and evening types. Aligning exposure to MSFsc broadly reversed the extreme-group differences seen in clock time. Morning types had higher exposure early in the local day, whereas evening types had higher post-MSFsc exposure. Morning-type exposure also declined earlier in clock time, yet was higher in the pre-MSFsc interval. The post-MSFsc difference was broadly similar on work and free days and remained visible under an alternative chronotype questionnaire. Exploratory daylength modeling also linked the average post-MSFsc contrast to photoperiod. Together, these results support considering daylight availability alongside individual sleep timing when describing chronotype-specific exposure.

The diary comparison supports using MSFsc as a reference for habitual sleep timing. Participant-average midsleep correlated more strongly with MSFsc than individual nights, and the modest work/free-day offsets followed the expected directions. Applying the sleep-debt correction to the diary means also brought their typical timing closer to questionnaire MSFsc, with a median difference of six minutes. The median within-person SD of 47 minutes nevertheless shows that actual midsleep varies around this reference. Consequently, the pre- and post-MSFsc exposure patterns describe group differences relative to habitual corrected midsleep while averaging over variation in nightly sleep schedules. The post-MSFsc interval broadly corresponds to the later part of habitual sleep, but does not identify the second half of every recorded sleep episode. Near awakening, this variation can change whether a given MSFsc-relative exposure occurs during sleep or wakefulness.

The established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure is the basis of the primary analysis. Its diary-derived correlate retained both directions of the exposure contrast, but the post-MSFsc daylength moderation was no longer significant. The same-participant questionnaire analysis retained significant moderation, so sample restriction alone does not explain this difference. Because dMSFsc changes both the timing alignment and quartile membership, the sensitivity cannot separate their contributions. It supports the exposure-pattern finding more consistently than the photoperiod association.

Later chronotypes encounter the dawn transition earlier relative to MSFsc. The civil-daylight summaries show more daylight for extreme morning types pre-MSFsc and extreme evening types post-MSFsc, matching the direction of both measured exposure differences. This timing agreement supports a daylight contribution to the post-MSFsc pattern. The pre-MSFsc interval-average comparison showed no significant photoperiod moderation. The photoperiod comparisons remain distinct: the gaps in astronomical daylight availability between morning and evening types narrowed on longer absolute days, whereas the average fitted evening-type/morning-type ratio increased with site-centered photoperiod. Indoor attenuation, artificial light and behavior determine how astronomical opportunity becomes measured exposure.

Natural-light camping studies provide complementary context: later chronotypes showed larger phase advances after a week outdoors, and seasonal and weekend changes in the light-dark environment altered melatonin timing.[@wright2013; @stothard2017] These interventions changed the whole light-dark environment and did not isolate a post-MSFsc photoperiod effect. Further, a mathematical model predicts that brighter daytime light narrows the distribution of circadian phase and sleep timing, with a stronger effect at longer photoperiods.[@papatsimpa2021]

The comparison with Goulet and colleagues is informative but not a direct replication.[@goulet2007] Their extreme-DLMO subset showed higher evening-type exposure at a later biological phase, qualitatively consistent with the post-MSFsc result here. Their morning-type excess near DLMO was not matched by a significant extreme-group interval within our external DLMO guide; our pre-MSFsc difference lay before it. The larger MeLiDos sample and near-eye melanopic measurements extend the evidence from Goulet and colleagues' wrist light recordings; their measured DLMO provided a more direct metric of circadian phase.

Emens and colleagues interpreted the greater advance-to-delay exposure balance in evening types as potentially meeting the greater daily advance needed to entrain a longer intrinsic circadian period.[@emens2009] This interpretation concerns the light input required to maintain stable entrainment, rather than evidence of progressive phase advancement. Our Emens-style sensitivity supported the relative evening-type/morning-type direction using broad, equally weighted phase windows, a different summary from the smooth PRC.

An ambulatory pilot study used a related approach, applying a nonlinear intensity–response transformation to personal illuminance before multiplying it by the Khalsa PRC and integrating advance and delay areas.[@arguellesprieto2022] Our use of log-transformed melanopic exposure, the one-hour PRC and MSFsc-based alignment is an adaptation of that approach. This precedent supports the weighting operation as a conceptual summary of exposure timing; it does not calibrate our index as a phase-shift prediction.

PRC weighting places extreme evening-type exposure in a relatively more phase-advancing direction and extreme morning-type exposure in a relatively more phase-delaying direction, but uncertainty in the direct group contrasts limits that interpretation. Raw-PRC group intervals spanned zero; drift correction yielded positive indices for both groups. The index also depends on exposure level and the reference assigned a neutral, zero contribution on the centered log scale (here 0 lux), because each PRC has nonzero signed area. Moreover, a laboratory response to one hour of bright white light cannot be treated as an additive dose–response function for naturally varying melanopic exposure. Thus the calculation is a structured comparison of timing, not a prediction of entrainment or a measured phase shift.

The relatively small allocation of fitted variation to chronotype and the absence of a predictive gain from daylength moderation put the group findings in context. Individual patterns accounted for much more of the fitted variation. MSFsc alignment is useful for examining when groups differ relative to their own sleep timing, while clock time retained slightly better prediction for new people. These results are compatible: an interpretable group contrast need not yield a better general-purpose predictor.

Several features constrain inference. The observational design cannot determine whether light exposure shaped chronotype, chronotype shaped exposure, or both reflected schedules and environments. Recruitment through research sites also limits population generalization. Extreme chronotypes overlapped poorly within sites; for example, no site contained at least five participants in both extreme groups. Site adjustment in the models accounts for shared site differences in the pooled estimate but cannot supply missing within-site comparisons.

Finally, near-eye recordings approximate the light environment without measuring retinal exposure, and bedside recordings during sleep do not incorporate eyelid transmission. DLMO and circadian phase shifts were not measured. A stronger test of the daylight explanation would observe both extreme groups at the same sites across seasons and measure DLMO. Such a design could, together with a separation of outdoor, indoor and sleep-associated exposure, distinguish daylight opportunity from behavior and test whether the post-MSFsc contrast translates into different circadian responses.

We asked whether chronotype differences persist after MSFsc alignment, vary with photoperiod and favor different phase-shifting directions. Extreme morning types had higher pre-MSFsc exposure, whereas extreme evening types had higher post-MSFsc exposure. With the established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure, photoperiod was significantly associated with the post-MSFsc contrast, with no significant pre-MSFsc moderation. The diary-derived correlate preserved the exposure differences but did not show significant post-MSFsc daylength moderation. The main PRC analysis suggested a relatively more phase-advancing evening-type pattern with uncertain group contrasts; our Emens-style sensitivity supported that relative direction. Together, these findings are compatible with a role for light exposure and photoperiod in moderating further advances or delays in extreme chronotypes, helping maintain stable 24-hour entrainment.
